title: What to do when…
intro: Small things that help, for the moments that are hard. Open any card, any time. You don't have to do all of it. One step counts.

cards.title: I want to text her
steps: Notice the urge. It feels like an emergency, but it's closer to withdrawal: your brain is used to her, and it wants its hit.
Wait 20 minutes. Urges rise, peak and fall, like a wave. You don't have to obey it to make it pass.
Write the message in your notes instead. Don't send it. Read it again tomorrow.
Text a friend or your sister instead: "I really want to text her right now." Saying it out loud takes half its power.

cards.title: I keep checking her profile
steps: Every check reopens the wound a little. It feels like information; it's mostly pain.
Mute or archive her. You don't have to block or make a statement. Just make checking take one more step.
Move the app off your home screen for a while.
When you catch yourself reaching for it, put the phone down and do one physical thing: stand up, drink water, step outside.

cards.title: A wave of sadness hits
steps: Don't fight it, don't fix it. Let it come.
Find where it is in your body: chest, throat, stomach. Put a hand there.
Let it be as big as it is. Cry if it comes. Feelings that are fully felt move through; feelings that are pushed away stay.
When it passes (it will), drink some water and do something small and kind for yourself.

cards.title: I keep finding her things
steps: Get a box.
For each thing, choose: give back, keep, or let go. There's no right answer.
Keeping a memory isn't holding on. Giving one away isn't forgetting.
Tape the box. Put it out of sight. It doesn't have to be today.

cards.title: I should be over it by now
steps: There is no deadline. "Should" is the Critic talking.
You don't have to get over her. You have to grieve her. Grief is love with nowhere to go for a while.
Notice if part of you is rushing to feel fine. Ask it, gently: what is it scared will happen if you're still sad?
Sad and okay can be true on the same day.

cards.title: Everything feels like too much
steps: Cold water on your face, and hold your breath for a few seconds. It tells your body to slow down.
Shake it out: hands, arms, shoulders, the whole body, for thirty seconds. Animals do this after a fright.
Breathe out longer than you breathe in. In for 4, out for 6, five times.
Pick one tiny thing: a glass of water, a shower, a walk round the block. Just that.
If it's more than you can carry, tap "I'm not okay" at the top.

cards.title: The voice in my head is mean
steps: Name it: "That's the Critic." It isn't the truth; it's a voice that thinks it's protecting you.
Get curious instead of arguing: what is it afraid of? Usually it's trying to stop you getting hurt again.
Ask yourself what you'd say to a friend who said this about himself. Say that.
You don't have to win against it. You just have to stop taking orders from it.

cards.title: I'm angry (at her, at myself)
steps: Anger is allowed. It's not the problem; acting on it at someone is.
Move it through your body, safely: walk fast, push hard against a wall, punch a pillow, shout into it in the car.
Let it be loud for a minute, alone. Anger that's felt cleanly tends to burn out, and what's under it shows up.
Ask: what is this anger protecting? Often it's hurt, or a line that got crossed.

cards.title: I can't sleep
steps: Phone out of reach. The scrolling feels like rest; it keeps your brain switched on.
Write down the worries on paper and give them an appointment: "I'll think about this tomorrow at 6."
If you're still awake after about 20 minutes, get up, sit somewhere dim and do something boring, then try again.
Get up at the same time tomorrow, even after a bad night. That's what resets sleep.

cards.title: I don't feel like doing anything
steps: You're not lazy. Low energy is part of heartbreak.
Don't wait for motivation. Motivation usually comes after you start, not before.
Make it two minutes: put shoes on, open the window, wash one plate.
Make it about someone else: it's easier to cook for someone than for yourself.

cards.title: It's evening and I'm alone
steps: Go where people are, even without talking to anyone: a café, a library, a bar with a match on.
Call or voice-message one person. Not to talk about her: just "what are you up to?"
Cook something real, with your hands. Make enough for two.
If it's a bad night, it's okay to just get through it. Tomorrow comes.

cards.title: I'm too scared to talk to people
steps: Fear isn't a stop sign. Everyone in the room feels some of it.
Prepare three lines in your pocket, like Théo: "First time here. How does this work?" works almost anywhere.
Ask one real question, then listen. People like the person who's curious about them.
If it goes badly, it's information, not a verdict. You did the hard part: you showed up.

cards.title: I don't know where to meet anyone
steps: Friendship is mostly showing up to the same place, at the same time, again and again.
Pick something with an activity: board games, a climbing gym, volunteering, a running club, a class. Doing something side by side is easier than face to face.
Go three times before you decide it's not for you. The first time everyone's a stranger; the third time you're a regular.
If nothing exists, start the small thing yourself: a note on the door, a pot of soup.

cards.title: A man shouldn't feel like this
steps: A lot of men grow up with one allowed feeling: anger. Everything else gets swallowed. It doesn't go away; it comes out sideways.
Sadness, fear and missing someone aren't weakness. They're information. Feeling them is what lets them pass.
Strength isn't not feeling it. It's feeling it, and still getting up, still being kind, still showing up.
Try saying the actual feeling out loud, to yourself or someone: "I'm sad." "I'm scared I'll be alone." Notice you're still standing.

cards.title: I don't have anyone to talk to
steps: This is really common for men, especially after a breakup: she was often the main person you talked to.
Men often bond side by side, doing something together. Invite someone to do a thing (a walk, a game, fixing something) rather than "to talk".
Go first with something small and true: "Honestly, it's been a rough month." Most friends are relieved, and open up too.
A therapist counts. Talking to a professional is training, not failure.

cards.title: I don't know who I am without her
steps: When a relationship ends, the plan for your life goes with it. Feeling lost is normal; it's not a sign you're broken.
Ask: who was I before her? What did I like when nobody was watching?
Purpose often comes from being useful to someone. Help a neighbour, cook, volunteer, teach something you know.
You don't need a plan yet. A direction is enough: towards people, towards things that make you curious.
